  pagetitle: "Hierarchical and Sleeve-Based Allocation"
  description-meta: "Optimizing within sleeves and then across them in R with PortfolioAnalytics: the two-stage problem, its reading as block-diagonal shrinkage, what mult.portfolio.spec() actually does, and whether the hierarchy survives out of sample."
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("R/_common.R")
library(tidypm)
library(knitr)
```

How should an allocation be organized when nobody can hold the whole problem
in one head, and what does the organization cost? @sharpe1981 posed it as the
decentralized investment problem, in which a central office sets budgets for
specialist managers who each optimize the sleeve they know and must be told
what makes the pieces add up, and @brinson1986 measured how much of an
institution's return that first, top-level decision explains. The two-layer
structure has been the working organization of every large allocator since:
classes first, then selection within them.

This is the chapter in which the book's own structure is made explicit. Parts
III to V allocate across the sixteen class series of
@sec-02-notation-and-data-simulated-market, and Part VI selects instruments
inside a sleeve; the two layers are not a convenience of exposition but a
decision with a cost, and the cost can be measured. It is a **strategic**
decision in the sense of @sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory: the
policy structure is set from unconditional assumptions and revisited rarely. We
first state the two-stage problem and read it as a shrinkage of the covariance
matrix, then implement it with `mult.portfolio.spec()` and by hand, then ask
whether the hierarchy dominates one-stage optimization out of sample on this
universe.

```{r}
#| label: data
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)   # 16 risky classes
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return                                  # the bill
Re <- R - rf                                                       # excess, @sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory
stopifnot(ncol(Re) == 16L, !anyNA(Re))
N  <- ncol(Re)
```

## The Two-Stage Problem {#sec-15-hierarchical-allocation-theory}

### Sleeves, and what is decided at each level

Partition the $N$ assets into $K$ sleeves and write the weight vector and the
covariance matrix in the same blocks,
$\boldsymbol{w} = (\boldsymbol{w}_1', \ldots, \boldsymbol{w}_K')'$ and
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = [\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{jk}]$. The one-stage, or **flat**,
problem is that of @markowitz1952 as stated in @sec-09-mean-variance-theory,
over all $N$ assets at once.
The two-stage, or **nested**, problem solves each sleeve on its own block first,

$$
\boldsymbol{v}_k = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{v}} \; \boldsymbol{v}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{kk}\boldsymbol{v}
\quad \text{subject to} \quad \boldsymbol{v}'\boldsymbol{\iota} = 1,\;
\boldsymbol{v} \geq \boldsymbol{0}, \qquad k = 1, \ldots, K,
$$ {#eq-15-stage1}

then treats each sleeve's portfolio as a single asset with return
$r_{k,t} = \boldsymbol{v}_k'\boldsymbol{r}_{k,t}$ and allocates across the
$K$ sleeve returns,

$$
\boldsymbol{b} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{b}} \; \boldsymbol{b}'\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{b}
\quad \text{subject to} \quad \boldsymbol{b}'\boldsymbol{\iota} = 1,\;
\boldsymbol{b} \geq \boldsymbol{0}, \qquad
\Omega_{jk} = \boldsymbol{v}_j'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{jk}\boldsymbol{v}_k .
$$ {#eq-15-stage2}

The portfolio that results holds, in every class, the sleeve budget times the
within-sleeve weight,

$$
\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{nest}} = (b_1 \boldsymbol{v}_1', \ldots, b_K \boldsymbol{v}_K')' .
$$ {#eq-15-unroll}

The objectives in @eq-15-stage1 and @eq-15-stage2 need not be the same; a
mandate can ask for minimum variance inside the bond sleeves and a tangency
portfolio inside equities, and @sec-15-hierarchical-allocation-application does
exactly that. What matters is the structure: nothing at stage 1 sees any asset
outside its own sleeve, and stage 2 sees the sleeves only through $K$ series.

@eq-15-unroll is feasible for the flat problem, so in sample the nested
portfolio can never have a lower variance than the flat minimum. The gap is the
price of decentralization. @vanbinsbergen2008 quantify it as a utility loss and
show that it is not small when the sleeve managers optimize against their own
objectives rather than the office's; @elton2004 derive the instructions, a
benchmark and a risk target for each sleeve, under which the decentralized
solution coincides with the centralized one; and @blake2013 document the
practice, in pension funds that split a balanced mandate into specialist
sleeves, gained on sleeve performance and paid in coordination. That the top
layer nonetheless carries most of the outcome is the finding of @brinson1986
and @brinson1991, which @ibbotson2000 restate carefully: policy explains about
ninety percent of a fund's variation over time, far less of the variation
between funds, and essentially all of the average level of return.

```{r}
#| label: sleeves
sleeve_of <- function(a) dplyr::case_when(
  grepl("_equity$", a)     ~ "equity",
  grepl("_government$", a) ~ "government",
  grepl("_credit$", a)     ~ "credit",
  TRUE                     ~ "commodity")

# split() returns its groups alphabetically; everything below indexes by name.
sleeves <- split(colnames(Re), sleeve_of(colnames(Re)))
stopifnot(setequal(unlist(sleeves), colnames(Re)))
lengths(sleeves)
```

Four sleeves: `r paste(names(sleeves), collapse = ", ")`. Three of them hold
five class series and the commodity sleeve holds one, which is a case the
implementation has to face rather than assume away.

### The shrinkage reading

Stage 1 of the nested problem uses only the diagonal blocks of
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$. It is therefore the flat problem solved on

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\text{B}} =
\begin{pmatrix}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11} & \boldsymbol{0} & \cdots \\
\boldsymbol{0} & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22} & \\
\vdots & & \ddots
\end{pmatrix},
$$ {#eq-15-block}

the matrix in which every cross-sleeve covariance has been set to zero. In the
language of @sec-07-covariance-matrix-theory that is a shrinkage estimator of
the form of @eq-07-shrinkage with a target that keeps the blocks and discards
the rest, and an intensity of one on the off-block entries and zero elsewhere.
The difference from @ledoit2004 is where the intensity comes from. Their
$\lambda$ minimizes expected loss and is estimated from the data; here it is
imposed by the mandate, and the justification is economic rather than
statistical: the cross-sleeve entries are the ones no sleeve manager is
responsible for, and stage 1 declares them unknown. What is known about
shrinkage since @stein1956 transfers directly. Setting parameters to zero helps
when their true values are near zero and their estimates are not, because those
are the entries the error-maximizer of @michaud1989 exploits, and hurts when it
discards information the portfolio was supposed to use.

Stage 2 restores part of that information, in coarse form. @eq-15-stage2 uses
the $K \times K$ matrix $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$, which carries $K(K-1)/2$
cross-sleeve covariances in place of the
$\sum_{j<k} N_j N_k$ that were dropped, and carries them only for the sleeve
compositions already fixed. If stage 2 ignores them as well, taking
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ to be diagonal, the top-level solution is
inverse-variance weighting across sleeves and the whole two-stage procedure
collapses to the flat minimum-variance portfolio of @eq-09-gmv computed on
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\text{B}}$:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\text{B}}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\iota} =
\big(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\iota},\, \ldots,\,
     \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{KK}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\iota}\big)'
\quad \Longrightarrow \quad
w_i = \frac{\sigma_k^{-2}}{\sum_{j} \sigma_j^{-2}}\, v_{k,i}
\;\; \text{for } i \in k,
\qquad \sigma_k^{2} = \frac{1}{\boldsymbol{\iota}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{kk}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\iota}} ,
$$ {#eq-15-identity}

because the inverse of a block-diagonal matrix is block-diagonal, and
$\sigma_k^2$ is sleeve $k$'s own minimum variance. The long-only version
separates the same way, given the sleeve budgets, and the worked box below
checks it numerically. So the three constructions form a ladder. The flat
problem uses every entry of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$; the nested problem uses the
diagonal blocks plus $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$; the block-diagonal problem uses the
diagonal blocks alone. Where nesting sits on that ladder depends on how much
of the cross-block covariance is signal.

```{r}
#| label: cross-block
S    <- stats::cov(Re)
same <- outer(sleeve_of(colnames(S)), sleeve_of(colnames(S)), "==")
stopifnot(all(dim(same) == dim(S)), isSymmetric(same))
S_block <- S; S_block[!same] <- 0

Cm <- stats::cov2cor(S)
c(cross_block_share = 1 - sum(S_block^2) / sum(S^2),          # of the Frobenius norm
  mean_within_cor   = mean(Cm[same  & upper.tri(Cm)]),
  mean_cross_cor    = mean(Cm[!same & upper.tri(Cm)]))
```

On the full sample the cross-sleeve entries carry
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (1 - sum(S_block^2) / sum(S^2)))` of the squared
mass of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, and the average correlation between two series
in different sleeves is `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(Cm[!same & upper.tri(Cm)]))`
against `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(Cm[same & upper.tri(Cm)]))` within a sleeve.
The blocks are real; the space between them is not empty. Whether the estimate
of that space is worth using is the question the out-of-sample race in
@sec-15-hierarchical-allocation-application answers, and the answer is in
keeping with @jagannathan2003 rather than with the usual case for shrinkage: a
restriction on the weights helps out of sample when it forbids what the
estimate gets most wrong, and the cross-sleeve covariances of sixteen classes
on sixty months are not that.

Everything in this chapter is the long-only quadratic program of
@sec-09-mean-variance-implementation, and the rolling loop of
@sec-15-hierarchical-allocation-application solves it more than a thousand
times, so we call `quadprog` directly, the solver `ROI` dispatches to in
@sec-13-solvers-implementation, and confirm once that the two agree.

```{r}
#| label: gmv-qp
gmv_qp <- function(S) {
  n   <- ncol(S)
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S, dvec = rep(0, n),
                            Amat = cbind(rep(1, n), diag(n)),
                            bvec = c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1)
  w <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  setNames(w / sum(w), colnames(S))
}

gmv_spec <- function(assets) {
  portfolio.spec(assets = assets) |>
    add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
    add.constraint(type = "long_only") |>
    add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var")
}

w_flat <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re, gmv_spec(colnames(Re)),
                                            optimize_method = "ROI"))[colnames(Re)]
stopifnot(max(abs(gmv_qp(S) - w_flat)) < 1e-8)

mu    <- colMeans(Re)
p_vol <- function(w) sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% S %*% w)) * sqrt(12)
p_ret <- function(w) sum(mu * w) * 12
p_sr  <- function(w) p_ret(w) / p_vol(w)
eff_bets <- function(w) 1 / sum(w^2)              # reciprocal Herfindahl, @sec-09
round(w_flat[w_flat > 0.005], 4)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked: the identity of @eq-15-identity, and the ladder in sample

Stage 1, stage 2 with a diagonal $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$, and @eq-15-unroll:

```{r}
#| label: identity-check
# A sleeve of one asset is its own portfolio.
within_gmv <- function(S, sleeves) lapply(sleeves, function(a)
  if (length(a) == 1L) setNames(1, a) else gmv_qp(S[a, a]))

unroll <- function(b, v) {
  stopifnot(identical(names(b), names(v)))
  w <- unlist(lapply(names(v), function(k) b[[k]] * v[[k]]))
  w[colnames(Re)]
}

v  <- within_gmv(S, sleeves)
s2 <- vapply(names(v), function(k)
  as.numeric(t(v[[k]]) %*% S[sleeves[[k]], sleeves[[k]]] %*% v[[k]]), numeric(1))
b_iv <- (1 / s2) / sum(1 / s2)                # inverse variance across sleeves

w_bd <- gmv_qp(S_block)                       # flat, on the block-diagonal matrix
stopifnot(max(abs(unroll(b_iv, v) - w_bd)) < 1e-10)
round(b_iv, 4)
```

The two-stage construction with inverse-variance budgets and the flat
minimum-variance portfolio on $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\text{B}}$ agree to
machine precision, under the long-only constraint. The nested portfolio proper
uses the full $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ at the top:

```{r}
#| label: nested-in-sample
sleeve_returns <- function(Re, v) {
  out <- do.call(cbind, lapply(names(v), function(k) Re[, sleeves[[k]]] %*% v[[k]]))
  colnames(out) <- names(v)
  xts::xts(out, order.by = zoo::index(Re))
}
sl       <- sleeve_returns(Re, v)
Omega    <- stats::cov(sl)
b_nest   <- gmv_qp(Omega)
w_nested <- unroll(b_nest, v)

Oc <- stats::cov2cor(Omega)
stopifnot(Oc["equity", "government"] < 0, sum(Oc[upper.tri(Oc)] < 0) == 1L)
round(Oc, 2)
```

The sleeve correlation matrix is where the discarded information reappears in
compressed form. Government and credit move together at
`r sprintf("%.2f", stats::cov2cor(Omega)["government", "credit"])`; equity and
government at `r sprintf("%.2f", stats::cov2cor(Omega)["equity", "government"])`,
the one negative entry, which is the entire reason a balanced portfolio holds
both. Stage 2 can act on it. Stage 1 could not, and chose the government sleeve
without knowing that the equity sleeve existed.

```{r}
#| label: ladder-in-sample
ladder <- tibble::tibble(
  construction = c("flat", "nested", "block-diagonal"),
  vol    = c(p_vol(w_flat), p_vol(w_nested), p_vol(w_bd)),
  sharpe = c(p_sr(w_flat),  p_sr(w_nested),  p_sr(w_bd)),
  bets   = c(eff_bets(w_flat), eff_bets(w_nested), eff_bets(w_bd)))
stopifnot(diff(ladder$vol) >= -1e-12)          # flat <= nested <= block-diagonal
ladder
```

The ordering is the one @eq-15-unroll guarantees, and the sizes are the point:
nesting costs `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * (ladder$vol[2] - ladder$vol[1]))`
percentage points of annualized volatility in sample, and dropping the
cross-sleeve covariances at both stages costs
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * (ladder$vol[3] - ladder$vol[1]))`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked: hierarchical risk parity is a different hierarchy

@lopezdeprado2016 uses the word *hierarchical* for a construction that has no
sleeves given to it. It estimates a tree from the correlation matrix, orders the
assets along that tree so that similar ones are adjacent, and allocates by
recursive bisection: split the ordered list in half, divide the budget between
the halves in inverse proportion to their variances, and recurse. Nothing is
inverted, which is why it was raised in
@sec-14-risk-based-allocation-application as the one popular method the
package lacks, and why it is defined even when @eq-07-rank makes
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ singular. @raffinot2018 examines the linkage and the
cut; @mantegna1999 is the origin of the correlation-distance tree in finance,
and @tola2008 the first use of such a tree to filter a covariance matrix
before optimizing on it.

```{r}
#| label: hrp
D  <- sqrt(0.5 * (1 - stats::cor(Re)))                  # the correlation distance
hc <- hclust(stats::as.dist(D), method = "single")
ord <- colnames(Re)[hc$order]                            # quasi-diagonalization

hrp <- function(S, ord) {
  iv_var <- function(items) {                            # inverse-variance variance
    s <- S[items, items, drop = FALSE]; iv <- 1 / diag(s); iv <- iv / sum(iv)
    as.numeric(t(iv) %*% s %*% iv)
  }
  w <- setNames(rep(1, length(ord)), ord)
  clusters <- list(ord)
  while (length(clusters)) {
    nxt <- list()
    for (cl in clusters) {
      if (length(cl) < 2L) next
      h <- floor(length(cl) / 2); a <- cl[1:h]; b <- cl[(h + 1):length(cl)]
      alpha <- 1 - iv_var(a) / (iv_var(a) + iv_var(b))
      w[a] <- w[a] * alpha; w[b] <- w[b] * (1 - alpha)
      nxt <- c(nxt, list(a), list(b))
    }
    clusters <- nxt
  }
  w[colnames(S)]
}
w_hrp <- hrp(S, ord)
stopifnot(abs(sum(w_hrp) - 1) < 1e-12)

# Is each country's credit series next to its own government series?
adjacent <- vapply(c("US", "UK", "EU", "CH", "JP"), function(cc)
  abs(match(paste0(cc, "_credit"), ord) - match(paste0(cc, "_government"), ord)) == 1L,
  logical(1))
stopifnot(sum(!adjacent) == 1L,                      # one exception, named below
          all(diff(sort(match(sleeves$equity, ord))) == 1L))   # the equities are contiguous
ord
```

Read the order. The estimated tree does not find the sleeves. It places the
credit series of `r c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five")[sum(adjacent)]` of
the five countries next to the same country's government series, with the
`r names(adjacent)[!adjacent]` pair the one exception, so the fixed-income half of
the universe is organized by currency rather than by asset class, which is
what @sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application measured:
unhedged in dollars, a foreign bond is mostly its currency. The asserted
hierarchy of this chapter and the estimated one of @lopezdeprado2016 disagree
about what a sleeve is, and the disagreement is a fact about hedging.

```{r}
#| label: hrp-summary
stopifnot(names(which.max(w_hrp)) == names(which.min(diag(S))))   # the prose says so
round(sort(w_hrp, decreasing = TRUE)[1:5], 4)
c(volatility = p_vol(w_hrp), effective_bets = eff_bets(w_hrp))
```

The portfolio it produces still puts
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * max(w_hrp))` in `r names(which.max(w_hrp))`, because
the bisection allocates by inverse variance and that series has the lowest
variance in the universe. The method changes how the hierarchy is found, not
what a low-volatility series does to an allocation.
:::

### The class series is the sleeve's benchmark

Each of the sixteen series is an index of the instruments inside it; the
equity series are the capitalization-weighted portfolios that
@sec-21-equity-sleeve-theory verifies against the instrument level, and
`US_government` stands in for a portfolio of Treasuries. That is what makes the
top layer a *policy*: it is set on investable proxies, in the manner of
@sharpe1992, and the weights it produces are handed down as benchmarks. The
sleeve manager then holds instruments and is judged, in
@sec-24-benchmarks-and-active-risk-theory, on the return in excess of that
benchmark and the tracking error it took. The class series is the sleeve's
benchmark, not its result. Setting the policy on a manager's realized returns
would reward each sleeve for the past alpha it will not repeat, carry that
selection into the backtest of @sec-25-backtesting-theory, and leave nothing
against which the manager could be judged; @roll1977 is the older statement
that the benchmark is a choice with consequences, and @grinold2000 the standard
account of what is measured once it has been made.

### Hedging is a sleeve decision

The sleeve structure also settles a question that has no answer at the level
of the whole portfolio. @sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application found that
hedging a Japanese government bond removes most of its volatility and hedging
Japanese equity removes almost none, and @campbell2010 show why the optimal
hedge differs systematically between bonds and equities: currencies covary
differently with each. A hedge is therefore a property of the sleeve rather
than of the country, and it changes what a sleeve holds.

```{r}
#| label: hedge-sleeves
fx <- sim_fx_monthly
hedged <- R
for (a in colnames(R)) {
  reg <- sub("_.*$", "", a)
  if (reg %in% unique(fx$region)) {
    f <- fx$fx_return[fx$region == reg][match(zoo::index(R), fx$date[fx$region == reg])]
    stopifnot(!anyNA(f))
    hedged[, a] <- R[, a] - f                  # hedged = unhedged - fx, @sec-04
  }
}
He <- hedged - rf

sleeve_vol <- function(X, a) {
  w <- gmv_qp(stats::cov(X[, a]))
  c(vol = sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% stats::cov(X[, a]) %*% w)) * sqrt(12),
    largest = max(w), bets = eff_bets(w))
}
hedge_tab <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c("government", "credit", "equity"), function(k)
  tibble::tibble(sleeve = k,
                 unhedged = sleeve_vol(Re, sleeves[[k]])[["vol"]],
                 hedged   = sleeve_vol(He, sleeves[[k]])[["vol"]],
                 bets_unhedged = sleeve_vol(Re, sleeves[[k]])[["bets"]],
                 bets_hedged   = sleeve_vol(He, sleeves[[k]])[["bets"]])))
gov <- hedge_tab[hedge_tab$sleeve == "government", ]
stopifnot(gov$hedged < gov$unhedged, gov$bets_hedged > gov$bets_unhedged)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-15-hedge
#| tbl-cap: "Minimum variance inside each sleeve, unhedged and fully hedged. Volatility annualized; effective bets are the reciprocal Herfindahl of the sleeve weights."
#| echo: false
hedge_tab |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(unhedged, hedged), ~ sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * .x)),
                dplyr::across(c(bets_unhedged, bets_hedged), ~ sprintf("%.2f", .x))) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrr",
        col.names = c("sleeve", "volatility, unhedged", "volatility, hedged",
                      "bets, unhedged", "bets, hedged"))
```

Hedging the government sleeve takes its minimum variance from
`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * hedge_tab$unhedged[hedge_tab$sleeve == "government"])`
to `r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * hedge_tab$hedged[hedge_tab$sleeve == "government"])`
and spreads it from
`r sprintf("%.1f", hedge_tab$bets_unhedged[hedge_tab$sleeve == "government"])` to
`r sprintf("%.1f", hedge_tab$bets_hedged[hedge_tab$sleeve == "government"])`
effective positions, because foreign bonds become holdable once their currency
is removed. Hedging the equity sleeve moves its volatility from
`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * hedge_tab$unhedged[hedge_tab$sleeve == "equity"])` to
`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * hedge_tab$hedged[hedge_tab$sleeve == "equity"])`.
@perold1988 and @black1989 are the two classic and opposed general answers;
the sleeve view makes the general answer unnecessary, and
@sec-22-fixed-income-sleeve-theory takes the bond side of it up where the
currency decision and the duration decision turn out not to be separable.

## Implementation {#sec-15-hierarchical-allocation-implementation}

`PortfolioAnalytics` has a data structure for this problem and almost no
documentation of it. `mult.portfolio.spec()` wraps a top-level specification,
`add.sub.portfolio()` attaches a sleeve specification together with the
settings used to optimize it, and `optimize.portfolio()` recognizes the result.
What it then does is not stated anywhere outside the source, so this section
reads the source and checks it against a by-hand construction.

### A sleeve of one asset

```{r}
#| label: one-asset
one <- try(optimize.portfolio(Re[, "GLOBAL_commodity", drop = FALSE],
                              gmv_spec("GLOBAL_commodity"), optimize_method = "ROI"),
           silent = TRUE)
stopifnot(inherits(one, "try-error"))
cat(conditionMessage(attr(one, "condition")))
```

::: {.callout-note}
## A single-asset sleeve cannot be a sub-portfolio

With one asset the constraint matrix loses a dimension on its way to
`ROI::L_constraint()`, which rejects it, and every rolling window of that
sleeve fails. The commodity sleeve therefore cannot enter
`mult.portfolio.spec()` at all. The package path below runs on the three
sleeves that can be optimized; the by-hand construction keeps the commodity as
a sleeve whose only asset is its portfolio, which is what
@eq-15-stage1 reduces to when $N_k = 1$.
:::

### `mult.portfolio.spec()` and `add.sub.portfolio()`

```{r}
#| label: mult-spec
three <- sleeves[c("equity", "government", "credit")]

top <- gmv_spec(names(three))
mp  <- mult.portfolio.spec(top)
for (k in names(three)) {
  mp <- add.sub.portfolio(mp, gmv_spec(three[[k]]), optimize_method = "ROI",
                          rebalance_on = "months", training_period = 60,
                          trailing_periods = 59)
}

c(class = class(mp), top = class(mp$top.portfolio)[1],
  sub_portfolios = length(mp$sub.portfolios), sub_class = class(mp$sub.portfolios[[1]]))
names(mp$sub.portfolios[[1]])
```

Three arguments are passed to every sub-portfolio, and none of them is
optional in practice. `optimize.portfolio()` on a `mult.portfolio.spec` calls
the unexported `proxy.mult.portfolio()`, whose loop is the whole of the method:

```r
for (i in 1:n.sub.portfolios) {
  tmp   <- mult.portfolio$sub.portfolios[[i]]
  R.tmp <- R[, names(tmp$portfolio$assets)]
  opt   <- do.call(optimize.portfolio.rebalancing, <R and the sub-portfolio's settings>)
  w     <- extractWeights(opt)
  ret[[i]] <- Return.portfolio(R.tmp, weights = w)     # named "proxy.i"
}
proxy.ret <- na.omit(do.call(cbind, ret))
```

after which `optimize.portfolio()` continues with `R <- proxy.ret` and
`portfolio <- portfolio$top.portfolio`. Every sleeve is run through
`optimize.portfolio.rebalancing()`, the rolling backtest of
@sec-25-backtesting-implementation, not through a single optimization; the
sleeve's returns are the realized returns of that backtest; and the top level
is optimized once, on the full history of those realized sleeve returns.

::: {.callout-important}
## The defaults do not run, and one argument is silently discarded

`add.sub.portfolio()` defaults `rebalance_on` to `NULL`, which
`optimize.portfolio.rebalancing()` passes to `xts::endpoints()`, which fails
with "missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed". A `mult.portfolio.spec` built
with the defaults cannot be optimized. Two further things about the settings.
`training_period = NULL` becomes thirty-six observations. And the length of
the window is `trailing_periods`, the argument `add.sub.portfolio()` names;
passing `rolling_window` instead, the name the rebalancing function itself
uses, looks as if it works and does not, because the sub-portfolio stores
`trailing_periods = NULL` alongside it and the rebalancing function's
compatibility shim overwrites `rolling_window` with that `NULL`. The result is
an expanding window that nothing reports. Both facts were established by
reproducing the proxy series by hand, below.
:::

```{r}
#| label: mult-default
mp_default <- mult.portfolio.spec(top)
for (k in names(three)) mp_default <- add.sub.portfolio(mp_default, gmv_spec(three[[k]]),
                                                        optimize_method = "ROI")
bad <- try(optimize.portfolio(Re, mp_default, optimize_method = "ROI"), silent = TRUE)
stopifnot(inherits(bad, "try-error"))
cat(strwrap(conditionMessage(attr(bad, "condition")), width = 78), sep = "\n")
```

```{r}
#| label: mult-run
#| cache: true
o_mp <- suppressWarnings(optimize.portfolio(Re, mp, optimize_method = "ROI", trace = TRUE))
round(o_mp$weights, 4)
c(proxy_rows = nrow(o_mp$R), proxy_cols = ncol(o_mp$R),
  first_model_year = model_year(zoo::index(o_mp$R)[1]),
  last_model_year  = model_year(zoo::index(o_mp$R)[nrow(o_mp$R)]))
```

Three things in that output need reading. The weights come back named
`proxy.1` to `proxy.3`, in the order the sub-portfolios were added, and the
names given to the top-level assets are ignored. With `trace = TRUE` the
object stores the proxy returns it optimized in `o_mp$R`, which is the only
way to see them. And they have `r nrow(o_mp$R)` rows, from
`r fmt_model(zoo::index(o_mp$R)[1])`, the first month of the sample, although
the first sleeve weights are estimated after sixty months. `Return.portfolio()` back-fills the training
period with an equally weighted, buy-and-hold sleeve, the behavior
@sec-23-rebalancing-implementation warns about, and the top level is estimated
on that history together with the rolling one.

### The same thing by hand

```{r}
#| label: mult-by-hand
W <- 60L
proxy_by_hand <- function(a) {
  X <- zoo::coredata(Re[, a, drop = FALSE]); n <- nrow(X); out <- numeric(n)
  w <- rep(1 / length(a), length(a))                  # the back-fill: equal, then drifting
  for (t in seq_len(W)) {
    out[t] <- sum(w * X[t, ]); w <- w * (1 + X[t, ]) / (1 + out[t])
  }
  for (t in (W + 1):n)                                # then rolling minimum variance
    out[t] <- sum(gmv_qp(stats::cov(X[(t - W):(t - 1), ])) * X[t, ])
  out
}
by_hand <- sapply(three, proxy_by_hand)
stopifnot(max(abs(zoo::coredata(o_mp$R) - by_hand)) < 1e-10)

b_hand <- gmv_qp(stats::cov(by_hand))
stopifnot(max(abs(as.numeric(o_mp$weights) - as.numeric(b_hand))) < 1e-6)

b_no_backfill <- gmv_qp(stats::cov(by_hand[-(1:W), ]))
round(rbind(package = as.numeric(o_mp$weights), by_hand = b_hand,
            without_backfill = b_no_backfill), 4)
```

The by-hand series reproduce the package's proxies to machine precision and
the top-level weights to the solver's tolerance, which is the documentation
this chapter set out to write. It also shows what the back-fill costs. Dropping
the sixty months nobody chose moves the government sleeve's budget from
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * b_hand[["government"]])` to
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * b_no_backfill[["government"]])`, a difference that is
not large here and that the package gives no way to remove.

### Holding several optimizations together

The stage-1 problems are ordinary `portfolio` objects, so their solutions can
be collected with `combine.optimizations()`, and `extractWeights()` on the
result is a matrix rather than a vector. On sleeve problems it is a picture of
@eq-15-block.

```{r}
#| label: sleeve-stage-list
ol_sleeves <- combine.optimizations(lapply(three, function(a)
  optimize.portfolio(Re[, a], gmv_spec(a), optimize_method = "ROI", trace = TRUE)))

W_sleeves <- extractWeights(ol_sleeves)
stopifnot(identical(rownames(W_sleeves), names(three)))
round(W_sleeves[, order(sleeve_of(colnames(W_sleeves)))], 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-15-sleeve-weights
#| fig-cap: "The three stage-1 solutions from `chart.Weights()` on an `opt.list`. Each line is one sleeve; a line is at zero outside its own block by construction."
#| fig-asp: 0.55
chart.Weights(ol_sleeves, main = "", legend.loc = "topleft", plot.type = "line")
```

The top-level problem takes the sleeve return series as its data, and several
candidate policies can be specified at once with `combine.portfolios()`, which
`optimize.portfolio()` solves in one call.

```{r}
#| label: top-list
qu_top <- gmv_spec(names(sleeves)) |> add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean")
qu_top$objectives[[1]]$risk_aversion <- 10        # gamma/2, @sec-91-proofs

policies <- combine.portfolios(list(
  `minimum variance`  = gmv_spec(names(sleeves)),
  `sleeve cap 50%`    = gmv_spec(names(sleeves)) |>
                          add.constraint(type = "box", min = 0, max = 0.5),
  `quadratic utility` = qu_top))

ol_top <- optimize.portfolio(sl, policies, optimize_method = "ROI", trace = TRUE)
names(ol_top) <- names(policies)               # the list's names are not carried over
stopifnot(inherits(ol_top, "opt.list"))

round(extractWeights(ol_top), 4)
round(extractObjectiveMeasures(ol_top), 5)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## `opt.list` methods need `trace = TRUE`

`extractObjectiveMeasures()` on an `opt.list` re-evaluates every objective in
the list on every portfolio, so that a minimum-variance solution acquires a
`mean` column when a return objective appears anywhere in the list. It reads
the returns from each element's `$R`, which exists only when the optimization
was run with `trace = TRUE`; without it the call fails with a message about an
argument of length zero. `chart.RiskReward()` goes through the same function
and fails the same way.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-15-top-riskreward
#| fig-cap: "Three top-level policies on the four sleeve series, from `chart.RiskReward()` on the `opt.list`. Circles are the sleeves themselves. Monthly units, not annualized."
#| fig-asp: 0.7
chart.RiskReward(ol_top, risk.col = "StdDev", return.col = "mean",
                 chart.assets = TRUE, main = "")
```

## Nested Against Flat {#sec-15-hierarchical-allocation-application}

### In sample

```{r}
#| label: in-sample
w_eq <- setNames(rep(1 / N, N), colnames(Re))
insample <- tibble::tibble(
  construction = c("flat minimum variance", "nested minimum variance",
                   "block-diagonal", "hierarchical risk parity", "equal weight"),
  vol    = c(p_vol(w_flat), p_vol(w_nested), p_vol(w_bd), p_vol(w_hrp), p_vol(w_eq)),
  ret    = c(p_ret(w_flat), p_ret(w_nested), p_ret(w_bd), p_ret(w_hrp), p_ret(w_eq)),
  sharpe = c(p_sr(w_flat),  p_sr(w_nested),  p_sr(w_bd),  p_sr(w_hrp),  p_sr(w_eq)),
  bets   = c(eff_bets(w_flat), eff_bets(w_nested), eff_bets(w_bd),
             eff_bets(w_hrp), eff_bets(w_eq)),
  top    = c(max(w_flat), max(w_nested), max(w_bd), max(w_hrp), max(w_eq)))
stopifnot(insample$sharpe[1] > insample$sharpe[2])   # nesting gives up Sharpe ratio in sample
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-15-insample
#| tbl-cap: "Five constructions on the full sample. Annualized, in excess of the bill; `largest` is the biggest single class weight."
#| echo: false
insample |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(vol, ret, top), ~ sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * .x)),
                sharpe = sprintf("%.3f", sharpe), bets = sprintf("%.2f", bets)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrrr",
        col.names = c("", "volatility", "excess return", "Sharpe", "effective bets", "largest"))
```

In sample the order is fixed by construction and @tbl-15-insample only
measures the gaps. Nesting gives up
`r sprintf("%.3f", insample$sharpe[1] - insample$sharpe[2])` of Sharpe ratio
against the flat solution and buys nothing visible in return: the nested
portfolio holds `r sprintf("%.2f", insample$bets[2])` effective positions
against the flat portfolio's `r sprintf("%.2f", insample$bets[1])`, with
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * insample$top[2])` in one series. The sleeve
structure did not diversify the answer, because @eq-15-stage2 is still a
minimum-variance problem and still buys the sleeve with the lowest variance;
what changes that is a constraint on the budgets, which is
@sec-12-constraints-theory's subject and the `sleeve cap 50%` row of the
`opt.list` above.

### Out of sample

The claim that matters is the one @sec-08-estimation-error-theory makes about
every method in this book: a restriction that costs variance in sample can buy
it back out of sample if what it forbids is mostly estimation error. We run the
four constructions on a sixty-month rolling window, monthly, from the same
first out-of-sample month as the register of `output/tables/oos-sweep.csv`, so
that the flat line can be checked against it.

```{r}
#| label: oos-loop
FIRST_OOS <- 121L                                # the register's first out-of-sample month
stopifnot(FIRST_OOS == which(model_year(zoo::index(Re)) == 11L)[1])   # first month of model year 11
oos    <- FIRST_OOS:nrow(Re)
rf_oos <- rf[oos]
Xm <- zoo::coredata(Re); Rm <- zoo::coredata(R)

race <- function(W) {
  paths <- lapply(oos, function(t) {
    X  <- Xm[(t - W):(t - 1), ]                    # the W months before t, nothing after
    Sw <- stats::cov(X)
    v  <- within_gmv(Sw, sleeves)
    sr <- sapply(names(v), function(k) X[, sleeves[[k]], drop = FALSE] %*% v[[k]])
    Sb <- Sw; Sb[!same] <- 0
    rbind(flat           = gmv_qp(Sw),
          nested         = unroll(gmv_qp(stats::cov(sr)), v),
          `block-diagonal` = gmv_qp(Sb),
          `equal weight` = rep(1 / N, N))
  })
  strategies <- rownames(paths[[1]])
  ret  <- sapply(strategies, function(s) vapply(seq_along(oos), function(i)
    sum(paths[[i]][s, ] * Rm[oos[i], ]), numeric(1)))
  # turnover against drifted end-of-period weights, as the register defines it
  turn <- sapply(strategies, function(s) {
    eop <- rep(0, N); out <- numeric(length(oos))
    for (i in seq_along(oos)) {
      w <- paths[[i]][s, ]; r <- Rm[oos[i], ]
      out[i] <- 0.5 * sum(abs(w - eop)); eop <- w * (1 + r) / (1 + sum(w * r))
    }
    mean(out) * 12
  })
  list(ret = ret, turnover = turn,
       sleeve_budget = sapply(seq_along(oos), function(i)
         tapply(paths[[i]]["nested", ], sleeve_of(colnames(Re)), sum)))
}

oos_stats <- function(r) {                       # the register's definitions
  n  <- length(r)
  ar <- prod(1 + r)^(12 / n) - 1
  af <- prod(1 + rf_oos)^(12 / n) - 1
  v  <- stats::sd(r) * sqrt(12)
  c(ann_return = ar, ann_vol = v, sharpe = (ar - af) / v)
}

race60 <- race(60L)
stats60 <- t(apply(race60$ret, 2, oos_stats))
round(cbind(stats60, turnover = race60$turnover), 4)
```

```{r}
#| label: oos-check
sweep <- utils::read.csv("output/tables/oos-sweep.csv") |>
  dplyr::filter(universe == "classes", frequency == "months", basis == "gross")
sweep_sr <- function(strategy, window) sweep$sharpe[sweep$strategy == strategy &
                                                     sweep$window == window]
stopifnot(abs(stats60["flat", "sharpe"] - sweep_sr("min_variance", 60)) < 0.05,
          abs(stats60["equal weight", "sharpe"] - sweep_sr("equal_weight", 60)) < 0.05)
c(flat_here = stats60["flat", "sharpe"], register = sweep_sr("min_variance", 60))
```

The flat line lands within
`r sprintf("%.3f", abs(stats60["flat", "sharpe"] - sweep_sr("min_variance", 60)))`
of the register's minimum-variance entry, which is the same problem solved by
`optimize.portfolio.rebalancing()` in @sec-25-backtesting-application, and the
equal-weight line reproduces it exactly, so the loop is scoring the same
months by the same definitions.

```{r}
#| label: oos-windows
windows <- c(36L, 60L, 120L)
by_window <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(windows, function(W) {
  s <- if (W == 60L) stats60 else t(apply(race(W)$ret, 2, oos_stats))
  tibble::tibble(window = W, construction = rownames(s),
                 sharpe = s[, "sharpe"], vol = s[, "ann_vol"])
}))
register_flat <- vapply(windows, function(W) sweep_sr("min_variance", W), numeric(1))
stopifnot(all(abs(by_window$sharpe[by_window$construction == "flat"] - register_flat) < 0.05))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-15-oos
#| tbl-cap: "Out-of-sample Sharpe ratios from the first month of model year 11, monthly rebalancing, for three estimation windows. The last row is the register's flat minimum-variance line, as a check."
#| echo: false
by_window |>
  dplyr::select(window, construction, sharpe) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = window, values_from = sharpe, names_prefix = "w") |>
  dplyr::bind_rows(tibble::tibble(construction = "register, flat",
                                  w36 = register_flat[1], w60 = register_flat[2],
                                  w120 = register_flat[3])) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(w36, w60, w120), ~ sprintf("%.3f", .x))) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr", col.names = c("", "36 months", "60 months", "120 months"))
```

```{r}
#| label: oos-verdict
#| include: false
gap60 <- stats60["flat", "sharpe"] - stats60["nested", "sharpe"]
nested_wins <- by_window |>
  dplyr::filter(construction %in% c("flat", "nested")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(id_cols = window, names_from = construction, values_from = sharpe) |>
  dplyr::summarise(n = sum(nested > flat)) |> dplyr::pull(n)
stopifnot(nested_wins == 0L)

# What the paragraph below states: flat has the lower realized volatility at sixty
# months, nested trails equal weighting there, block-diagonal trails nested at every
# window, and the stage-1 loss exceeds the stage-2 recovery.
bd_vs_nested <- by_window |>
  dplyr::filter(construction %in% c("nested", "block-diagonal")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(id_cols = window, names_from = construction, values_from = sharpe)
stopifnot(stats60["flat", "ann_vol"] < stats60["nested", "ann_vol"],
          stats60["nested", "sharpe"] < stats60["equal weight", "sharpe"],
          all(bd_vs_nested$`block-diagonal` < bd_vs_nested$nested),
          gap60 > stats60["nested", "sharpe"] - stats60["block-diagonal", "sharpe"])
```

The hierarchy does not dominate one-stage optimization out of sample on this
universe. That is worth pausing on, because the nested rule estimates fewer
covariances than the flat one, and the finding of @demiguel2009 that the book
has met at every turn is that rules which estimate less tend to do better out
of sample. At sixty months the nested construction earns a Sharpe ratio of
`r sprintf("%.3f", stats60["nested", "sharpe"])` against the flat
portfolio's `r sprintf("%.3f", stats60["flat", "sharpe"])`, a gap of
`r sprintf("%.3f", gap60)`, and the flat portfolio also has the lower realized
volatility, `r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * stats60["flat", "ann_vol"])` against
`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * stats60["nested", "ann_vol"])`. The nested portfolio
finishes behind equal weighting as well. Shortening the window to thirty-six
months, which makes every estimate worse and should favor the construction
that estimates fewer covariances, does not reverse the order, and neither does
lengthening it to one hundred and twenty. The block-diagonal construction
trails the nested one at every window, which places the two on the ladder of
@sec-15-hierarchical-allocation-theory: what stage 2 recovers through
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ is worth
`r sprintf("%.3f", stats60["nested", "sharpe"] - stats60["block-diagonal", "sharpe"])`
of Sharpe ratio at sixty months, and what stage 1 discards is worth more.

That is the shrinkage reading confirmed from the other side. @ledoit2004 shrink
because the sample matrix is badly conditioned, and on sixteen series and sixty
months it is not: @sec-07-covariance-matrix-theory found no rank-deficient
window in thirty-one model years at class level. The cross-sleeve covariances are
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (1 - sum(S_block^2) / sum(S^2)))` of the matrix and,
at this dimension, mostly information. The case for a hierarchy that discards
them is the case @sec-07-covariance-matrix-implementation made for holding
fewer things, and it arrives when the flat matrix cannot be estimated at all,
which is the situation of @sec-21-equity-sleeve-theory and not of this
chapter. Here the structure is a governance decision, and the table prices it.

```{r}
#| label: fig-15-oos-cumulative
#| fig-cap: "Growth of one unit of excess return, sixty-month window, monthly rebalancing, out of sample from model year 11. One frame, log scale. The flat and nested lines part gradually, in no single episode, and never rejoin."
#| echo: false
#| fig-asp: 0.6
growth <- tibble::tibble(
  date = rep(zoo::index(Re)[oos], times = ncol(race60$ret)),
  construction = rep(colnames(race60$ret), each = length(oos)),
  excess = as.vector(race60$ret) - rep(rf_oos, times = ncol(race60$ret))) |>
  dplyr::group_by(construction) |>
  dplyr::mutate(growth = cumprod(1 + excess)) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()
stopifnot(nrow(growth) == length(oos) * ncol(race60$ret))

# The caption's claim: the gap is positive at the end, and no named episode of
# `sim_episodes` accounts for as much as half of it.
gap <- growth |>
  dplyr::filter(construction %in% c("flat", "nested")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(id_cols = date, names_from = construction, values_from = growth) |>
  dplyr::mutate(gap = log(flat / nested))
episode_share <- vapply(sim_episodes$episode, function(e) {
  i <- which(in_episode(gap$date, e))
  (gap$gap[max(i)] - c(0, gap$gap)[min(i)]) / gap$gap[nrow(gap)]
}, numeric(1))
stopifnot(gap$gap[nrow(gap)] > 0, all(episode_share < 0.5))

ggplot2::ggplot(growth, ggplot2::aes(date, growth, colour = construction)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_log10() +
  scale_x_model() +
  scale_colour_tidyaa() +
  ggplot2::labs(y = "growth of 1, excess of the bill (log scale)")
```

```{r}
#| label: sleeve-budget-path
budget <- t(race60$sleeve_budget)
round(colMeans(budget), 3)
```

@fig-15-oos-cumulative shows the gap opening steadily rather than in any one
episode: the largest share any named episode of `sim_episodes` contributes to
it is `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * max(episode_share))`, in the
`r sim_episodes$label[which.max(episode_share)]`. The sleeve budgets show why
it does not close. Averaged over the out-of-sample period the nested
construction gives the government sleeve
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * colMeans(budget)[["government"]])` of the portfolio
and the equity sleeve
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * colMeans(budget)[["equity"]])`. Inside the
government sleeve, stage 1 chose the composition on government covariances
alone; the flat problem chose its government holdings for how they sit against
equities, and that is the part of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ stage 1 never sees.
Turnover, which @sec-23-rebalancing-application prices, is
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * race60$turnover[["nested"]])` a year for the nested
construction against `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * race60$turnover[["flat"]])` for
the flat one, so costs do not change the ranking.

### The policy view

A policy is not usually minimum variance everywhere. The structure of
@eq-15-stage1 and @eq-15-stage2 lets each level carry its own objective, and
the combination a mandate most often asks for is a tangency portfolio where
returns are believed to be forecastable and minimum variance where they are
not. The long-only tangency portfolio is one quadratic program, minimum
variance at unit expected return, rescaled to a full budget; it is the point
@eq-09-tangency picks out, and rather than scanning a frontier for it as
@sec-09-mean-variance-implementation does we solve it directly and check it
against a scan of forty frontier points on the sleeve series.

```{r}
#| label: tangency-qp
tan_qp <- function(S, mu) {
  stopifnot(any(mu > 0))
  n   <- ncol(S)
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S, dvec = rep(0, n),
                            Amat = cbind(mu, diag(n)), bvec = c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1)
  w <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  setNames(w / sum(w), colnames(S))
}

# the check: no long-only frontier portfolio has a higher Sharpe ratio
S_sl <- stats::cov(sl); mu_sl <- colMeans(sl); n_sl <- ncol(sl)
sr_of <- function(w) sum(mu_sl * w) / sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% S_sl %*% w))
scan <- vapply(seq(min(mu_sl), max(mu_sl), length.out = 42)[2:41], function(target) {
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S_sl, dvec = rep(0, n_sl),
                            Amat = cbind(rep(1, n_sl), mu_sl, diag(n_sl)),
                            bvec = c(1, target, rep(0, n_sl)), meq = 2)
  sr_of(sol$solution)
}, numeric(1))
stopifnot(sr_of(tan_qp(S_sl, mu_sl)) >= max(scan) - 1e-8)
c(tangency = sr_of(tan_qp(S_sl, mu_sl)) * sqrt(12), best_of_scan = max(scan) * sqrt(12))
```

```{r}
#| label: policy
v_policy <- list(
  equity     = tan_qp(S[sleeves$equity, sleeves$equity], mu[sleeves$equity]),
  government = gmv_qp(S[sleeves$government, sleeves$government]),
  credit     = gmv_qp(S[sleeves$credit, sleeves$credit]),
  commodity  = c(GLOBAL_commodity = 1))
v_policy <- v_policy[names(sleeves)]

sl_policy <- sleeve_returns(Re, v_policy)
b_policy  <- tan_qp(stats::cov(sl_policy), colMeans(sl_policy))
w_policy  <- unroll(b_policy, v_policy)
stopifnot(abs(sum(w_policy) - 1) < 1e-10)

within_all <- unlist(v_policy)                    # names are "sleeve.class"
policy <- tibble::tibble(class = colnames(Re), sleeve = sleeve_of(colnames(Re))) |>
  dplyr::mutate(within = unname(within_all[paste0(sleeve, ".", class)]),
                budget = unname(b_policy[sleeve]),
                weight = budget * within) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(budget), dplyr::desc(weight))
stopifnot(!anyNA(policy$within),
          max(abs(policy$weight[match(colnames(Re), policy$class)] - w_policy)) < 1e-12)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-15-policy
#| tbl-cap: "The nested policy read as a strategic asset allocation: sleeve budget times within-sleeve weight is the class weight, and the class weights are what the sleeve managers receive as benchmarks. Classes with a weight below half a percent omitted."
#| echo: false
policy |>
  dplyr::filter(weight >= 0.005) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(within, budget, weight), ~ sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * .x))) |>
  kable(align = "llrrr",
        col.names = c("sleeve", "class", "within-sleeve weight", "sleeve budget", "class weight"))
```

```{r}
#| label: policy-summary
w_flat_tan <- tan_qp(S, mu)
c(policy_sharpe = p_sr(w_policy), flat_tangency_sharpe = p_sr(w_flat_tan),
  policy_vol = p_vol(w_policy), sleeves_held = sum(b_policy > 0.005))
```

@tbl-15-policy is what a strategic asset allocation looks like as a document,
the policy portfolio that @ang2014 places at the center of institutional
practice:
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * b_policy[["government"]])` to the government sleeve,
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * b_policy[["equity"]])` to equity, and inside each a
regional split the sleeve manager inherits. The equity manager of
@sec-21-equity-sleeve-theory receives the five regional weights in the equity
rows as a benchmark and selects instruments against it; the fixed-income
manager of @sec-22-fixed-income-sleeve-theory receives the government rows and
a hedging instruction with them. The policy earns an in-sample Sharpe ratio of
`r sprintf("%.3f", p_sr(w_policy))` against `r sprintf("%.3f", p_sr(w_flat_tan))`
for the flat tangency portfolio, and after @sec-09-mean-variance-application
neither number should be read as a forecast. The anchored variant of this
problem, in which the sleeve manager optimizes around the benchmark under a
tracking-error budget rather than from scratch, is a different formulation
and belongs to @sec-24-benchmarks-and-active-risk-implementation.

## Key Takeaways {.unnumbered}

- The nested problem of @eq-15-stage1 and @eq-15-stage2 is the structure every
  large allocator uses, and @sharpe1981 posed the question it raises: what
  the top level must tell the sleeves so that the parts add up. In sample it
  can never dominate the flat problem, because @eq-15-unroll is feasible for
  it.
- Stage 1 is the flat problem on the block-diagonal matrix of @eq-15-block: a
  shrinkage estimator whose intensity is set by the mandate rather than
  estimated. With inverse-variance budgets at the top, the two constructions
  coincide exactly, by @eq-15-identity.
- `mult.portfolio.spec()` runs each sleeve through the rolling backtest of
  `optimize.portfolio.rebalancing()`, back-fills the training period with a
  drifting equal-weight sleeve, and optimizes the top level once on the
  result. Its defaults do not run, `rolling_window` is silently discarded in
  favor of `trailing_periods`, a one-asset sleeve cannot be optimized, and
  the proxy series are visible only with `trace = TRUE`.
- On sixteen classes and a sixty-month window the hierarchy loses out of
  sample, at every window length tried, and the block-diagonal construction
  loses by more. At this dimension the cross-sleeve covariances are
  information rather than noise; the case for discarding them arrives at
  instrument level, where the flat matrix cannot be estimated.
- The estimated hierarchy of hierarchical risk parity groups fixed income by
  currency rather than by class, which is the hedging decision of
  @campbell2010 seen from the data: a hedge is a property of the sleeve, and
  it changes what the bond sleeves hold while leaving the equity sleeve alone.
- The class series is the sleeve's benchmark. The policy is set on investable
  proxies and handed down; the sleeve manager is judged against it.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. The tree in the hierarchical-risk-parity box grouped the bond series by
   currency. Build the sleeves that way instead, one sleeve per currency with
   the commodity on its own, and rerun `race(60L)`. Does the currency
   hierarchy dominate the class hierarchy out of sample, and does either
   dominate the flat construction?
2. Replace the top-level minimum-variance step in `race()` with the
   inverse-variance rule of @eq-15-identity and confirm, window by window,
   that the result coincides with the block-diagonal line to machine
   precision. Then say in one sentence what the difference between the nested
   and block-diagonal rows of @tbl-15-oos measures.
3. Repeat the hierarchical-risk-parity construction with complete linkage in
   place of single linkage and cut the tree at four clusters. Does the
   estimated hierarchy recover the four sleeves? Report the cross-tabulation of
   clusters against sleeves.
4. The package back-fills the first `training_period` months of every proxy
   with a buy-and-hold equal-weight sleeve. Using `proxy_by_hand()`, vary the
   training period over 36, 60 and 120 months and report how far the top-level
   weights move when the back-filled months are dropped. At which window does
   the back-fill matter most, and why?
